stem: A client has anemia with an elevated mean corpuscular volume (MCV). Which deficiency pattern should the nurse consider?

options.A: Iron deficiency, which characteristically produces macrocytosis as iron stores fall.
options.B: Thalassemia trait, which characteristically produces a high MCV from enlarged red blood cells.
options.C: Vitamin B12 or folate deficiency, which can produce megaloblastic macrocytic anemia.
options.D: Anemia of chronic disease, which is defined by marked macrocytosis from folate trapping.

rationale: ARUP Consult defines megaloblastic anemia as a form of macrocytic anemia and notes that macrocytosis, commonly an MCV above 100 fL, may prompt evaluation. Major causes include vitamin B12 or folate deficiency, although medications and other disorders can also produce macrocytosis. Therefore C is correct as a deficiency pattern to consider. Iron deficiency and thalassemia more commonly produce microcytic patterns, and anemia of chronic disease is not defined by marked macrocytosis from folate trapping.
educational_objective: Recognize vitamin B12 and folate deficiency as important causes of megaloblastic macrocytic anemia when an elevated MCV is identified.
source_version_date: Megaloblastic Anemia last updated August 2024; ARUP Consult currentness live-rechecked August 16, 2026
source_locator: Megaloblastic Anemia > Overview/Quick Answers: megaloblastic anemia is macrocytic; anemia with macrocytosis (MCV >100 fL) prompts evaluation; vitamin B12 or folate deficiency are major causes. Anemia topic: high MCV differential includes folate/B12 deficiency; iron deficiency is typically microcytic.
source_claim_supported: An elevated MCV indicates macrocytosis, and vitamin B12 or folate deficiency should be considered because either can cause megaloblastic macrocytic anemia.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Reduction of Risk Potential: interpret hematologic laboratory findings, identify abnormal red-cell indices, and recognize potential nutritional causes requiring additional evaluation.
blueprint_topic: Reduction of Risk Potential — macrocytic anemia and vitamin-deficiency evaluation

source_original.stem: A client has anemia with an elevated mean corpuscular volume (MCV). Which deficiency pattern should be considered?

options.A: Iron deficiency, which characteristically produces macrocytosis as iron stores fall.
options.B: Thalassemia trait, which characteristically produces a high MCV from enlarged red cells.
options.C: Vitamin B12 or folate deficiency, which can produce megaloblastic macrocytic anemia.
options.D: Anemia of chronic disease, which is defined by marked macrocytosis from folate trapping.

source_original.rationale: An MCV above the reference range indicates macrocytosis. Low vitamin B12 or folate can cause macrocytic or megaloblastic anemia, whereas iron deficiency more commonly produces microcytosis.
source_original.source_detail: Macrocytic/megaloblastic anemia evaluation: increased MCV and vitamin B12 or folate deficiency. Live ARUP Consult topic currentness rechecked 2026-08-15. NCSBN first-check: Client Needs — Physiological Integrity — Reduction of Risk Potential: diagnostic/laboratory interpretation, transfusion risk, postprocedure monitoring, device management and potential complications. 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan; effective 2026-04-01 through 2029-03-31; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.

correction_summary: Retained the macrocytic-anemia construct and key C. No clinical correction to the answer was needed; reduced difficulty from hard to easy because the final item tests a direct red-cell-index/deficiency association.

audit_findings.source_authority: Current ARUP Consult hematology guidance; NCSBN 2026 blueprint
audit_findings.currentness: ARUP Consult Megaloblastic Anemia and Anemia topics live-rechecked 2026-08-16
audit_findings.exact_locator: ARUP Megaloblastic Anemia overview/Quick Answers and Anemia MCV differential
audit_findings.claim_audit: Final item asks which deficiency pattern should be considered rather than claiming that elevated MCV proves B12/folate deficiency; it preserves other possible macrocytosis causes.

distractor_audit.A: Incorrect because iron deficiency characteristically causes microcytosis rather than macrocytosis.
distractor_audit.B: Incorrect because thalassemia trait is typically microcytic, not high-MCV macrocytic.
distractor_audit.D: Incorrect because anemia of chronic disease is not defined by marked macrocytosis from folate trapping.

audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: Only C is a deficiency pattern classically associated with megaloblastic macrocytic anemia.
audit_findings.cueing: All options are anemia etiologies/deficiency interpretations tied to MCV.
audit_findings.blueprint: Reduction of Risk Potential — hematologic laboratory interpretation.
audit_findings.independent_second_pass: Rechecked current ARUP macrocytosis/megaloblastic anemia guidance, all options, rationale, objective, non-diagnostic wording, ambiguity, cueing and NCSBN mapping. C remained uniquely correct.
